tldr: By freezing a pretrained MoE whole-body control policy and training attachable task-specific experts with only about 1% of the base actor's parameters, this method enables humanoid robots to continually acquire challenging new skills without degrading any existing motions.
hero_caption: Overall concept of the proposed PERA framework. The base pretrained policy remains completely frozen, and independent task experts are trained and called on demand for each new skill. Turning the switch off fully restores the original computation path of the base policy.
overview:
Motion imitation has become a powerful tool for teaching humanoid robots diverse whole-body skills like walking and dancing. However, when faced with new tasks involving novel contact patterns or posture constraints—such as leaping over obstacles or climbing—fine-tuning the entire model causes catastrophic forgetting, damaging existing skills. On the other hand, training and maintaining a separate giant controller for every single task drastically inflates storage and maintenance costs.

To solve this, the authors developed PERA. It keeps a pretrained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) policy completely frozen and only trains a tiny task expert module and its routing score for each new task. The new module adds only about 1.03% of the base actor's parameters, yet it efficiently learns by reusing existing motion representations. Furthermore, an explicit switch can toggle the module on or off during inference; disabling it restores the original computation path 100%.

In experiments using the Unitree G1 simulation, plugging PERA modules into the frozen base policy enabled the robot to complete all 10 challenging parkour-style tasks. Disabling the expert perfectly preserved all 126 base motions. Interestingly, enabling the expert also improved tracking accuracy on fast dance motions that were never seen during its training, showing compelling generalization capabilities.
contributions: Proposed an expert expansion architecture that allows robots to independently acquire new skills with tiny parameter overhead (approx. 1.03%) while keeping the pretrained MoE base policy completely frozen.

Designed a plug-in structure supporting both reinforcement learning (PPO) and imitation learning (BC + online DAgger), featuring an explicit ON/OFF switch that fully restores the original computation path and existing behaviors.

Demonstrated 100% completion across 10 challenging new tasks on Unitree G1, improved generalization on unseen fast dance motions, and showed strong adaptability across different base policies including HoloMotion.

sections.heading: How can we add new skills without breaking existing ones?
sections.summary: In humanoid whole-body control, updating the entire model degrades existing motions, while training separate models per task causes storage and maintenance headaches. PERA solves this dilemma by keeping the pretrained policy frozen and plugging in tiny, dedicated experts.
sections.details:
In recent years, reference motion imitation has enabled humanoid robots to perform dynamic behaviors such as walking, jumping, and dancing using a single policy. However, when encountering new tasks with unseen obstacles or specialized contact constraints, existing motion tracking capabilities often fall short.

Naively fine-tuning the entire policy overwrites shared parameters, degrading or altering hard-won existing motions. Conversely, training and storing a separate full controller for every new task severely strains storage and prevents the reuse of shared whole-body representations.

To address this challenge, the authors propose freezing the base policy and plugging in task-specific modules only when needed. In a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) structure, experts share feature extraction and output layers while coordinating through a router. This means that by training a new expert and its dedicated routing score independently, one can add new skills on top of shared base representations without corrupting existing knowledge.

At the core of PERA, existing parameters are never updated during new task training. An explicit switch is provided at runtime, instantly and completely restoring the base policy's original behavior simply by turning the expert off.

captions.F1: Conceptual overview of PERA. With the base policy (bottom left) frozen, independent task experts are trained and added for each new skill, such as dive rolling or climbing. An explicit switch allows plugging the required expert into the existing control loop instantly.

sections.heading: At the intersection of whole-body control, continual learning, and MoE
sections.summary: This section reviews advances in whole-body motion imitation, continual learning for robotics, MoE, and module integration. PERA stands out by freezing a pretrained foundation and expanding it independently, rather than training a monolithic policy from scratch.
sections.details:
### Whole-body motion control
Beginning with DeepMimic and progressing through PHC, SONIC, and KungfuBot2, combining large-scale motion datasets with reinforcement learning has rapidly expanded whole-body humanoid capabilities. While these works focus on packing as many skills as possible into a single monolithic policy, PERA takes a different perspective: how to independently add new experts on top of an already established base policy.

### Continual skill learning
Prior works have explored combining LoRA and progressive neural networks based on motion similarity (LoRA-PNN), building dynamic experts from multi-task pretraining (LiMoDE), and using lightweight routers with coefficient replay (DMPEL). PERA also belongs to the continual learning family, but is distinguished by its strictly plug-and-play design that keeps base parameters fully frozen.

### Expert modules and knowledge integration
Approaches in this space include MoE-Loco (avoiding gradient conflicts across terrains using MoE), FlexOlmo (fusing independently trained experts at inference), and CPC (repeated distillation from teacher models). PERA draws on these concepts and introduces a competitive routing mechanism where the new expert competes and cooperates with existing ones.

### Pretrained control policies
Recent frameworks include HoloMotion-1, which learns a sparse Transformer-based MoE from video and MoCap data, and SuperMimic, which leverages a differentiable world model to boost sample efficiency. PERA's base policy follows the design principles of SuperMimic, and experiments further validate its extensibility using HoloMotion-1 as an alternative base.

sections.heading: How do we plug a new expert into a frozen policy?
sections.summary: PERA completely freezes the base model—including its encoder, decoder, and output layers—and only trains a new task expert (FFN) and its routing score. It optimizes the module using PPO task rewards or DAgger teacher supervision, integrating it into control via competitive Top-2 selection.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Pretrained whole-body motion tracking policy
The base policy follows the SuperMimic architecture. It encodes a reference motion target window $g_t$ and combines it with the last 10 steps of proprioceptive observations $o_{t-9:t}$ in a decoder to output control features. These features are processed by a shared expert and routed experts, finally generating a 29-dimensional joint action $a_t \in \mathbb{R}^{29}$ through an output head. After pretraining with a differentiable world model, the encoder, decoder, eight routed experts, one shared expert, output head, and normalization statistics are all frozen completely.

### 3.2 Task expert training
When learning a new task, a new feedforward network (FFN) expert is initialized by copying the weights of an existing expert. During training, gradients only flow into and update this newly added FFN and its scoring branch.

The router assigns a raw logit $\ell_i$ to each candidate expert and adds a fixed bias $\delta_i$ to compute a selection score $v_i = \ell_i + \delta_i$. When the new expert is enabled, the top 2 experts are selected from the 9 total candidates (8 existing + 1 new), with ties broken in favor of existing experts. The mixing weights $\omega_i$ for the selected two experts are computed via a softmax over their raw scores $\ell_i$ (without bias), and their weighted features are passed to the output head. The shared expert is always active.

Two training modalities are supported:
- **Reward-based learning (PPO):** When an explicit task reward can be designed, trajectories are collected in simulation, and the added module is optimized directly using PPO. A separate critic network is trained alongside it.
- **Teacher supervision (BC + online DAgger):** When a reliable teacher policy is available, behavioral cloning (BC) first imitates teacher actions, followed by online DAgger where the teacher labels states visited by the policy itself.

### 3.3 Expert invocation and base policy restoration
The added expert, its scoring branch, and selection bias are saved independently with a very lightweight footprint. At runtime, turning the switch off completely bypasses the added module, restoring the base policy's original routing and computation path 100%. Because base weights and normalization statistics remain untouched, the output actions match the original policy identically for any given input.

captions.F2: Training and inference pipeline of PERA. (a) Only the added FFN and its routing score are updated, using either BC + DAgger from teacher actions or reinforcement learning (PPO). (b) During inference, Top-2 experts are competitively selected from 8 existing + 1 new experts; turning the switch OFF instantly restores the original routing.

sections.heading: Conquering 10 hard tasks with surprising generalization
sections.summary: Evaluated on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 simulator, PERA added only ~1.03% in parameters yet cleared all 10 parkour tasks. Disabling the module preserved 100% of the 126 original motions, while enabling it boosted completion on unseen fast dance motions from 59.38% to 71.88%.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Evaluation setup and base policy
Experiments were conducted in simulation using the Unitree G1, a 29-degree-of-freedom humanoid robot. The base actor network contains approximately 10.4M parameters, comprising 8 routed experts and 1 shared expert. The added task expert module accounts for only about 1.03% of the base actor's parameter count.

The new tasks come from the Deep Whole-body Parkour dataset, covering 10 demanding motions (S01 to S10) with varying terrains and obstacles, such as dive rolling, kneel climbing, jump sitting, and roll vaulting. The control frequency is 50 Hz.

### 4.2 Retention and transfer to unseen motions
First, disabling the expert was evaluated across all 126 original motions used in pretraining. The outputs matched the base policy identically, maintaining a 100% success rate and identical tracking errors (proving zero catastrophic forgetting).

Next, to see how the expert affects motions beyond its training data, the robot executed 8 fast dance motions never used to train the expert. Enabling the expert increased the proportion of fully completed episodes from 59.38% to 71.88%, and raised the average motion completion rate from 73.24% to 83.83%. This indicates that the expert trained on extreme parkour tasks provides generalized capabilities in posture control and dynamics compensation under demanding conditions.

### 4.3 Generalization across base policies (evaluation with HoloMotion)
To confirm that PERA is not tied to a single base architecture, it was applied to HoloMotion-1, a policy trained under a different paradigm. Across all 10 tasks, average termination position error dropped sharply from 173.36 cm to 28.51 cm, and average root position error improved from 15.12 cm to 14.37 cm.

Furthermore, across 5 tasks where all 16 evaluation episodes completed successfully, HoloMotion + PERA was compared against the teacher policy. It achieved 27.40% lower termination position error and 14.70% lower root position error on average, outperforming the teacher's tracking accuracy in 4 out of the 5 tasks.

captions.F3: Generalization evaluation on unseen fast dance motions not used during expert training. (a) Completed episode ratio increased from 59.38% to 71.88%, and (b) average completion rate rose from 73.24% to 83.83%. (c) On the most improved motion, joint error decreased by 7.10% and body position error by 31.51%.
captions.F4: Task error comparison between different base models (authors' base model vs. HoloMotion-1). Blue bars (positive values) indicate lower errors for HoloMotion + PERA, showing that different base policies exhibit different task strengths.
captions.F5: Tracking error comparison against the teacher model across the 5 tasks completed by both policies. (a) Error reduction rate per task (blue indicates beating the teacher), and (b) average error comparison across the 5 tasks. HoloMotion + PERA reduced termination position error by 27.40% and root position error by 14.70% relative to the teacher.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A plug-in path toward lifelong robot control
sections.summary: PERA combines full retention of existing capabilities with accurate acquisition of new skills by attaching minimal experts to a frozen policy. Demonstrating broad compatibility with different bases and positive transfer to unseen motions, it offers a practical roadmap for lifelong robot skill expansion.
sections.details:
This paper presented PERA, a framework for retrofitting task experts onto a pretrained whole-body motion control policy. Each task module is trained independently, participating in control by competing and cooperating with existing experts. When not needed, switching it off completely restores the original behavior of the base model.

In evaluations on the Unitree G1, adding only ~1.03% in parameters enabled the robot to conquer 10 challenging parkour tasks while retaining 100% performance on all 126 original motions. It also produced the welcome side effect of improving tracking on unseen fast dance motions. Experiments with HoloMotion further confirmed that this approach serves as a general expansion platform, independent of specific policy architectures.

Looking ahead, this points toward modular lifelong learning systems where robots can simply download and plug in specialized skill modules for diverse field tasks without ever retraining their core models.

takeaways: Freezing the base model and adding an MoE expert with only ~1% of parameters completely prevents catastrophic forgetting while acquiring hard skills.
An explicit ON/OFF switch provides deterministic safety by fully reproducing the exact base policy outputs when disabled.
Adding specialized experts yields positive transfer, improving posture control even on unseen fast dynamic motions like dancing.
Applicable not only to custom architectures but also directly to external pretrained policies like HoloMotion.
limitations: Validation is limited to the Unitree G1 simulation environment; robustness to real-world contact impacts and actuator delays (Sim-to-Real) has not been demonstrated directly.
As independent experts accumulate, automated rules for module selection and storage management when scaling to hundreds or thousands of tasks remain undefined.
Learning new tasks strictly requires explicit reward design or high-quality teacher policies (for DAgger), making upfront supervision data preparation a bottleneck.
